dervis-irab:1-9.t:
* Vocabulary:
(هُمَزَةٍ): In al-Mukhtār: «al-hamz is like al-lamz in pattern and meaning, and its verb-class is that of ḍaraba.» Also in it: «al-lamz is finding fault; its origin is signalling with the eye and the like; its verb-class is that of ḍaraba and naṣara.» The tāʾ in both is for intensification of the description. It has preceded that the pattern fuʿala, with ḍamma on the fāʾ and fatḥa on the ʿayn, is for intensification of the agent, i.e. one who does much of what the word is derived from, and the pattern fuʿla, with ḍamma on the fāʾ and sukūn on the ʿayn, is for intensification of the object. One says «رجل لُعَنة» (luʿana), with ḍamma on the lām and fatḥa on the ʿayn, of one who curses others much, and «لُعْنة» (luʿna), with ḍamma on the lām and sukūn on the ʿayn, when he is cursed by people, who curse him much. Al-Samīn's wording: «The generality [of readers] read both with fatḥa on the mīm, meaning the person from whom that act comes much; the others read with sukūn, meaning the one who [gives cause to be] slandered and backbitten, i.e. who brings what he is slandered and backbitten for — like ḍuḥaka of one who laughs much and ḍuḥka of one who does what is laughed at. It is regular, I mean that fuʿala with fatḥa on the ʿayn is for one from whom the act comes much, and with sukūn for one on account of whom the act occurs much.»
Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «The hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa] in "همزة" entered for intensification of blame, as in their saying "rajul humaza lumaza", i.e. a fault-finder and backbiter; and "rajul farūqa, ṣakhkhāba, jakhkhāba": one of much talk and quarrelling; "naqqāqa, mihdhāra, halbāja". Al-Aṣmaʿī said: I asked a Bedouin about the halbāja and he said: he is the tall, bulky fool, very meddlesome, gluttonous, ill-mannered — and if you stopped [me], I would [go on] describing him until tomorrow; there is nothing among faults worse than the halbāja. Since the hāʾ entered for that [purpose], masculine and feminine became equal, so it is said "a woman humaza" and "a man humaza", "a woman farūqa" and "a man farūqa", and it is not put in the dual or plural: one says "men humaza" and "women humaza". The grammarians said: when they put the hāʾ on [an epithet of] one who is praised, they take it in the sense of the shrewd one possessed of irba, which is intelligence, as it is said "rajul ʿallāma" and "nassāba"; and when they put the hāʾ on [an epithet of] one who is blamed, they take it in the sense of the beast. Similar is His saying "بل الإنسان على نفسه بصيرة": the hāʾ is for intensification; and similar is the saying of the Exalted "ولا تزال تطلع على خائنة منهم": the hāʾ is for intensification. And he recited:
تدلي بودّي إذا لاقيتني كذبا ... وإن أغيب فأنت الهافر اللمزه
(You falsely lay claim to my affection when you meet me, but if I am absent, you are the backbiter, the fault-finder.)
Al-hāfir is the backbiter and al-lāmiz is the fault-finder. Allah the Exalted said: "ومنهم من يلمزك في الصدقات", i.e. strikes at you (yuṣībuka).» [Translator's note: «يصيبك» as printed; «يعيبك» (finds fault with you) would be expected.] What we have extracted from the books of language is the following inflection of the two.
One says: hamazahu yahmuzuhu (with ḍamma on the mīm) and yahmizuhu (with kasra), hamzan: he poked him, pressed him, prodded him, pushed him, struck him, bit him, and backbit him in his absence; so he is hammāz and humaza, [like] kasra [Translator's note: so in the text; the pattern-word is presumably a misprint]. Hamaza al-shayṭānu al-insāna: he whispered an insinuation into his heart. Hamaza bihi al-arḍa: he threw him to the ground. Hamaza al-farasa: he prodded the horse with the spur (al-mihmāz) so that it would run. Hamaza al-ʿinaba or its head: he pressed it. Hamaza al-kalimata or al-ḥarfa: he pronounced it with a hamza or put the sign of the hamza on it.
And one says: lamazahu yalmuzuhu (with ḍamma on the mīm) and yalmizuhu (with kasra), lamzan: he found fault with him, signalled at him with his eye and the like together with hidden speech, pushed him and struck him; lamazahu al-shaybu: grey hair appeared in him. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: «Al-humaza is the one who strikes (yahmizu) people with his hand and beats them, and al-lumaza is the one who slanders (yalmizu) them with his tongue and finds fault with them.» Ibn Kaysān said: al-humaza is the one who hurts his companion with foul speech, and al-lumaza is the one who winks his eye, gestures with his head and signals with his eyebrow. There are other views, all of which go back to a single root, namely attacking and exposing faults.
(عَدَّدَهُ): Al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, said: «The generality [of readers] read with the first dāl doubled, which is also for intensification; al-Ḥasan and al-Kalbī read it lightened. Whoever doubled its mīm looked to intensification and multiplication, and whoever lightened its mīm made it admit multiplication and its absence.» [Translator's note: «ميمه» (its mīm) as printed; the letter in question is the dāl.] The meaning is: he amassed it, kept count of it and reckoned it up.
(لَيُنْبَذَنَّ): he will surely be thrown. Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «The meaning of "ينبذن" is: he will be left in Hell. Allah the Exalted said: "فنبذوه وراء ظهورهم", i.e. they left it. The foundling child (al-ṣabiyy al-manbūdh) is the one left [abandoned]; he is [also called] the child of motion, al-mudaghdagh, and the son of the night, i.e. the child of the wicked woman; and he is al-nufl and the son of al-musāʿāt — all of it [meaning] the child of fornication.»
(الْحُطَمَةِ): one of the names of the Fire, i.e. that which smashes everything thrown into it. In al-Mukhtār: «ḥaṭamahu, of the verb-class of ḍaraba, i.e. he broke it, so it broke (inḥaṭama, taḥaṭṭama); al-taḥṭīm is breaking; al-ḥuṭama is one of the names of the Fire, because it smashes what it swallows.»
(مُؤْصَدَةٌ): closed over. [The poet] said:
تحنّ إلى جبال مكة ناقتي ... ومن دونها أبواب صنعاء مؤصدة
(My she-camel yearns for the mountains of Mecca, while before them the gates of Ṣanʿāʾ are shut.)
(عَمَدٍ): it was read with two fatḥas, with two ḍammas, and with ḍamma then sukūn. The first two are plurals of ʿamūd. In the books of language: al-ʿamūd is that on which the house and other things stand, and a rod of iron; the plural is aʿmida, ʿamad and ʿumud. The third is a lightening of the reading ʿumud with two ḍammas. Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «Al-ʿamad is the plural of ʿamūd. Nothing has come in the speech of the Arabs on this pattern except four words: adīm and adam, ʿamūd and ʿamad, afīq and afaq, ihāb and ahab. Al-Farrāʾ added a fifth: qaḍīm and qaḍam, meaning parchments and skins. The people of Kufa read "في عُمُد" with two ḍammas, which is also the plural of ʿamūd, like rasūl and rusul. Hārūn related from Abū ʿAmr "في عُمْد" with sukūn on the mīm, as a lightening, like rasūl and rusl.»

* I'rab:
(وَيْلٌ لِكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُمَزَةٍ الَّذِي جَمَعَ مالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ): «ويل» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and «لكل همزة» is its khabar (predicate). What permitted beginning with it although it is indefinite is the sense it contains of invoking destruction upon them. Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «If someone asks: "ويل" is indefinite, and one does not begin with an indefinite noun, so what accounts for the nominative? Say: when the indefinite comes close to the definite, it is fit to begin with, as in "Better than Zayd is a man of the Banū Tamīm" and "A man in the house is standing". Likewise the interrogative alif makes beginning with the indefinite easy, as in His saying [sic] "أمنطلق أخوك". This is one view. Others said: "ويل" is definite, because it is the name of a valley in Hell — we seek refuge with Allah from it. If it is said: Did the Arabs know that? Say: the words of the Qurʾān come as an Arabic word used figuratively, just as Allah the Exalted called the idol "Baʿl" when it was taken as a lord, and called the idol "punishment" and "rujz", saying "والرجز فاهجر", because whoever worships the idol is struck by the rujz (punishment), so it was named by the name of what it causes. So since al-wayl is destruction and ruin, and whoever enters the Fire has perished, it is permissible to call the destination of al-wayl "wayl". Likewise "فسوف يلقون غيا" — it is said to be a valley in Hell, we seek refuge with Allah from it. In grammar "ويلاً لكل همزة" is permissible as an invocation, i.e. may Allah make woe cling to him. Jarīr said:
كسا اللؤم تيما خضرة في جلودها ... فويلا لتيم من سرابيلها الخضر
(Baseness has clothed Taym with a greenness in their skins, so woe to Taym from its green shirts!)
— with the accusative, the correct transmission. The Kufans allowed wayl, wayli, waylu and waylan, whether the annexation is cut off or intended. Al-ways is a word lighter than al-wayl, al-wayḥ is a word lighter than al-ways, and al-wayb is a word lighter than al-wayḥ: "wayl li-Zayd", "waylahu", "wayḥahu", "waysahu", "waybahu". When it stands alone, the nominative and the accusative are both permissible; when it is annexed, it can only be accusative, because it would remain without a khabar; and when it is separated, you make the lām [phrase] the khabar. Al-Ḥasan said: "wayḥ" is a word of mercy. If it is said: how is a verb inflected from wayḥ, ways and wayl? Say: the Arabs did not inflect a verb from them. As for this fabricated verse:
فما وال وما واح ... وما واس أبو زيد
(Abū Zayd did not say "wayl", nor "wayḥ", nor "ways".)
— pay no attention to it, for it is a vile fabrication.»
«لمزة» is a badal (substitute) of «همزة». This is Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «"لمزة" is a substitute of it. Al-mihmaza is a stick with a piece of iron at its tip, carried by the horse-breaker, with which he prods the riding animal; the plural is mahāmiz. ʿAdī said, describing a horse:
نصفه جوزه نصير شواه ... مكرم من مهامز الرّوّاض
(We describe its middle [?] and its legs; it is spared the spurs of the horse-breakers.) [Translator's note: the first hemistich is obscure as printed; the gloss is tentative.]
And Abū Muḥallim recited:
هل غير همز ولمز للصديق ولا ... ينكي عدوكم منكم أظافير»
(Is there anything but prodding and slandering of the friend, while your enemy is not wounded by any claws of yours?)
It is also said [that «لمزة»] is a verbal tawkīd (emphasis) of «همزة» by a synonym. «الذي» is a badal of «كل», a substitution of a definite for an indefinite, or it is accusative by an omitted verb, as blame. Ibn Khālawayh parsed it as a naʿt (adjective) of «كل همزة لمزة», and that is not far-fetched. The clause «جمع» is the ṣila (relative clause) of «الذي», with no grammatical position; the agent of «جمع» is latent, its implied form being «هو», referring to «كل همزة لمزة»; «مالا» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); and «عدده» is conjoined to «جمع». Ibn Khālawayh's wording: «"وعدده" is coordinated (nasaq) with it; the maṣdar is ʿaddada yuʿaddidu taʿdīdan, so he is muʿaddid; and the hāʾ is a direct object. Al-Ḥasan read "جمع مالا وعَدَدَه" lightened, i.e. he amassed wealth and knew its number and reckoned it up. Whoever lightened it made al-ʿadad a maṣdar and a noun, and whoever doubled it made it a past verb.» This is one view on the meaning of the lightened [reading]. It is also said: and he gathered his own ʿadad (supporting numbers) of his clan and kinsmen; on this interpretation it is likewise a noun, conjoined to «مالا», i.e. and he amassed the number of the wealth, or the number of his own [people]. It is also said that «عدده» [lightened] is a past verb meaning «عدّه» (he counted it), except that it is anomalous in being left unassimilated, the regular form being assimilation, just as the poet was anomalous in his saying: «إني أجود لأقوام وإن ضنّوا» (I am generous to people even if they are stingy) — i.e. bakhilū [with «ضننوا» unassimilated in the original].
(يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ): the clause is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the agent of «جمع», i.e. reckoning and supposing that wealth will make him immortal, i.e. bring him to the rank of immortality so that he will not die. It may also be resumptive, an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) answering a question, as if it were said: what is the matter with him that he amasses wealth and is concerned with it? «أن» and its noun, and the clause «أخلده» is its khabar; and «أن» with what is in its domain stands in place of the two objects of «يحسب». In al-Mukhtār: «al-khuld, with ḍamma, is permanence; its verb-class is that of dakhala; akhladahu Allāhu and khalladahu takhlīdan.»
(كَلَّا لَيُنْبَذَنَّ فِي الْحُطَمَةِ وَما أَدْراكَ مَا الْحُطَمَةُ نارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ): «كلا» is deterrence and rebuke of him for his supposition, i.e. the matter is not as passed through his mind, that wealth will make him immortal. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath; «ينبذنّ» is an imperfect passive verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa because of its being attached to the heavy nūn of emphasis; its nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent, its implied form being «هو»; the clause has no grammatical position because it is the answer to the oath; and «في الحطمة» is attached (mutaʿalliq) to «ينبذنّ». The wāw is a conjunction; «ما» is an interrogative noun in the position of a nominative, mubtadaʾ; the clause «أدراك» is a verbal clause in the position of a nominative, khabar; «ما» is an interrogative noun, mubtadaʾ, and «الحطمة» is the khabar; and the nominal clause, suspended [from the verb] by the interrogative, stands in place of the second object of «أدراك». Many parallels to it have preceded. «نار الله» is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. «هي نار الله», and «الموقدة» is an adjective of «النار». Ibn Khālawayh allowed it to be a badal of «الحطمة», with «الموقدة» an adjective of «نار الله». His wording:
«"نار الله الموقدة": if you wish, you make "النار" a substitute; and if you wish, you make it nominative as the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e. "هي نار الله". The name of Allah the Exalted is genitive by annexation, and "الموقدة" is an adjective of "النار"; its pattern is mufʿala, from awqadtu, ūqidu, īqādan, so I am mūqid and the fire is mūqada. And the fire itself waqadat, taqidu, waqdan and wuqūdan (with ḍamma on the wāw), so it is wāqida. Allah the Exalted said: "وقودها الناس والحجارة", meaning sulphur stones; al-waqūd with fatḥa is firewood. Ṭalḥa read "وُقودها" with ḍamma on the wāw, making it a maṣdar. The poet — Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī — said:
ليلك يا موقد ليل قرّ ... والريح مع ذلك ريح صرّ
أوقد يرى نارك من يمرّ ... إن جلبت ضيفا فأنت حر
(O kindler of the fire, your night is a cold night, and the wind besides is a biting wind; kindle [it], so that whoever passes may see your fire — if you bring in a guest, you are free.)
This is the best that has been said on its meaning.»
(الَّتِي تَطَّلِعُ عَلَى الْأَفْئِدَةِ): «التي» is an adjective of «النار»; it may also be in the position of a nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. The clause «تطّلع» is the ṣila of «التي», with no grammatical position; the agent of «تطّلع» is «هي», referring to the Fire; and «على الأفئدة» is attached to «تطّلع». The pattern of «تطّلع» is tafṭaʿil: the tāʾ of iftiʿāl was changed to ṭāʾ because it came after a ṭāʾ; it is likewise changed to ṭāʾ when [the first radical] is ṣād, ḍād or ẓāʾ. ʿUrwa ibn Udhayna said:
عاود القلب خيال ردعه ... كلما قلت تناهى اطلعه
يا له داء ترى صاحبه ... ساهم الوجه له ممتقعه
(A phantom returned to the heart, a phantom that had been held back; whenever I said it had ceased, it came to view again. What a malady! You see the one afflicted by it with a lean face, pallid on its account.)
(إِنَّها عَلَيْهِمْ مُؤْصَدَةٌ فِي عَمَدٍ مُمَدَّدَةٍ): «إن» and its noun; «عليهم» is attached to «مؤصدة»; «في عمد» is an adjective of «مؤصدة» — this is the view Abū al-Baqāʾ took, so that the Fire is inside the columns. It is also said [it is attached] to an omitted [word], the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ. Al-Samīn preferred that it be a ḥāl of the pronoun in «عليهم», i.e. bound fast. «ممددة» is an adjective of «العمد».

* Rhetoric:
In His saying «لينبذنّ في الحطمة» after «ويل لكل همزة لمزة» there is a verbal correspondence (muqābala lafẓiyya) of splendid eloquence. For when He branded him with this mark, in a form indicating that it is deep-rooted in him and has taken firm hold of him, He followed the repeated intensification in «الهمزة» and «اللمزة» with His threat of the Fire, which He named «الحطمة» because of the terror he suffers in it and the punishment he meets in it. In specifying it He chose an intensive form on the pattern of the form in which He couched the sin committed, so that equivalence is achieved between sin and recompense: this one who became addicted to sin, his recompense is this ḥuṭama, which is also ravenous, smashing everything thrown into it. It is said that this sūra was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq, whose habit was backbiting and slander; it is also said about Umayya ibn Khalaf; and it is said about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and his backbiting of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his disparagement of him. Even if the occasion was specific, the threat was general, covering everyone who bears this base mark, so that it functions as an innuendo (taʿrīḍ) at the one about whom it was revealed, for that is a stronger deterrent to him and wounds him more deeply. The discussion of taʿrīḍ has passed: it consists in a person alluding by one thing to another without stating it explicitly, so that the hearer takes it to himself and knows what is meant by it — as when someone says «How ugly is stinginess!», so [the hearer] knows that you meant to tell him: you are stingy; and as when someone said to another: «My mother was not an adulteress», insinuating that the other's mother was an adulteress. Taʿrīḍ is in any case a kind of kināya (allusion). Among its poetic examples is the saying of al-Ḥajjāj, insinuating against the governors who preceded him:
لست براعي إبل ولا غنم ... ولا بجزار على ظهر وضم
(I am no herdsman of camels or sheep, nor a butcher at the back of a chopping-block.)
